warmup.text: Jack and Praiseworthy step off the boat into San Francisco, and everything costs too much. Before you read, answer the question on the card. Then read a galloping poem out loud and listen for the hoofbeats.

words.text: Write four sentences that join ideas with and, but, because, although or when. Find the run and pull roots hiding in new words. Then listen for the loud beat in the shun words. Eight more planks for the furnace today.

reading.text: Read Chapter 8, Saved by a Whisker. Watch the prices. Then watch a shaggy stranger, and one small choice that changes everything for Jack and Praiseworthy.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 8. Then keep drafting your middle. If you get stuck, use the frames: first, then, finally.

cards.title: Real history: the ships left in the harbor
cards.intro: The Lady Wilma and the Sea Raven are made up. The crowded harbor in Chapter 8 was real.

items.term: Crews ran off to the gold fields
items.meaning: In 1849 ship after ship sailed into San Francisco Bay, and many crews left for the gold fields as soon as they landed. Hundreds of empty ships sat in the cove. Some were pulled up onto the mud and used as stores, warehouses, hotels and even a jail.

In Chapter 8 a hotel runner shouts, Try the Niantic Hotel. The Niantic was a real ship. It sailed into the bay on July 5, 1849, and within a week its crew was gone. It was hauled ashore and used as a store and warehouse. After a fire in 1851, the Niantic Hotel was built on top of what was left of it, so Fleischman borrowed the hotel's name two years early.

The town filled in the shallow cove with sand, and old ships ended up blocks from the water, under new streets. Workers dug up a large part of the Niantic in 1978, and a piece of its stern is in San Francisco's maritime museum today.

cards.note: Source: National Park Service, San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park.

cards.title: A note before you read: words from 1963
cards.intro: This book was written in 1963. A few lines in Chapter 8 describe people in ways that are unkind and untrue. Here is what to know.

items.term: How the book describes Chinese people
items.meaning: Chapter 8 calls the Chinese people on the wharf silent and calls their braids pigtails, and it writes the laundryman's English as broken speech. Many books from that time made Chinese people into a joke this way. It is unfair to real people.

Chinese immigrants began arriving in California in 1849 and soon numbered in the thousands. Many men wore a long braid called a queue, because the rulers of China required it. Chinese workers ran laundries, cooked, mined and later helped build the railroad, and they faced unfair laws, such as special taxes on foreign miners that began in 1850.
Quartz Jackson thanks Praiseworthy by saying it is mighty white of him. It is an old saying that treats being white as the same as being good. It is a racist phrase, and we do not use it.

cards.note: When you meet these lines, notice them. The book shows what many people believed then, not what is true.

art.title: San Francisco in July, 1849
art.alt: A painting of a small town of white houses and tents spreading down hills to a bay crowded with ships' masts, with riders and miners camping in the front.
art.look: George Henry Burgess was in San Francisco during the Gold Rush. He painted this view in 1891 from his memories and sketches of July 1849, the same summer Jack and Praiseworthy land. Look at the forest of masts in the bay, the tents on the hillside, and how new and scattered the town still looks.
